doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Jazz as a language: accents, Parker and Mulligan
summary: Players have accents; swing and bebop are not used up, and solos need logic whether technical like Parker or sparse like Mulligan or Baker.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah. Okay. Yeah. Okay. So anyway, we speak the American English language and if we hear somebody speaking that language with an accent, if we’re a student of the language if we really know it well we can identify the accent. Like in jazz there might be more of a blues accent sometimes. There might be more of a so-called cool accent in other players. There might be some players that in the course of their phrases they’re constantly changing from reaching many different levels of volume, from the softest notes in the music to the loudest, and then other people that even though they’re convincing soloists, their dynamic level is not so variable, and stays pretty much — even in Baroque music. I mean with the instruments that they had there is not a huge dynamic range. So if there’s one element that doesn’t have so much to offer in the music you have to make up for it by doing more with those other elements. But then we can also tell in a minute if somebody’s an immigrant — speaking English with a foreign accent — or, either an immigrant or a native speaker, that just doesn’t know the language very well and they’re making lots of grammatical mistakes or speaking in fragments or speaking in a dissociative, almost schizophrenic way, leaping from one theme to another without any notice or any connection. And you can make an analogy between all these things and playing a jazz solo or writing a big band arrangement or a composition. And the thing that I think is the greatest danger for the music is when people get the idea that well why should I play swing music? You know, that’s all been done. Louis Armstrong already did all that. Why should I play bebop? You know, Charlie Parker did all that. But no, that’s not true at all. That’s like saying that we have to invent a new language because everything has already been written in English that can be thought of. That’s absolutely not the case. And everybody today still, if you want to be a poet or a short story writer or a playwright or a novelist or a social critic, philosopher, whatever, you’re going to use American English. But the fact that everybody uses American English doesn’t mean that it’s impossible to eventually develop your own voice in the way that you use that language in the way you develop the subject matter that you want to discuss and go into. So I mean to me it would be a real tragedy because we’re so interested in creating something new all the time. I mean it’s mostly novelty for it’s own sake from what I’ve found. And when we go back, especially when we listen to not only people that play in a fairly technical way, like Charlie Parker. I mean he’s a great example of somebody that © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

sometimes played a lot of notes, but when you really painstakingly learn one of the Parker solos, you can hear that every one of those notes make sense, and that one phrase really has something to do with the phrase before or with the phrase that’s coming afterwards. And very often the key notes in those phrases, the top note or the longest note, may even be the note that happens to be there in the original melody. But you have to get to more than just a completely superficial understanding of music before you start to recognize these things. But on the other hand, then there are people like, well Gerry Mulligan, for example, or Chet Baker, who use far less notes and play slightly different tone color. And in a certain way they’re making solos not from the more technical vocabulary than Parker and Gillespie and Bud Powell evolved in the bebop era, but from melodic material that you associate with the riffs of swing tunes and with melodies from the American Popular Songbook. But the thing that both of those styles have and that they have in common with Louis Armstrong or any meaningful jazz that’s happened in the last fifty years is that there is a real logic and integrity within the soloing, just like a nice short story or a poem. It has a clear beginning, middle and end, and once you hear what the soloist has to say in that first phrase, if you pay attention everything that comes after that has something to do with what came before.
